description:
## Description
This figure displays weight visualizations of maxout networks trained on the MNIST dataset. Each row represents the filters for a single maxout unit. The left panel shows the filters of a naively trained model, while the right panel shows the filters of a model trained with adversarial examples. The visualizations highlight the differences in filter patterns between the two models.

## Text in figure
- Left panel: "Naively trained model"
- Right panel: "Model with adversarial training"

Figure: Line plot showing the argument to softmax against ε.

Description: The plot displays multiple lines, each representing a different series labeled from 0 to 9. The series labeled 0 is the highest, reaching approximately 1000, while series 9 is the lowest, starting near -2000. The lines intersect at a point near ε = 0.

Text in figure: ε, argument to softmax, series labels 0 to 9.

caption: Figure 4: By tracing out different values of ϵ , we can see that adversarial examples occur reliably for almost any sufficiently large value of ϵ provided that we move in the correct direction. Correct classifications occur only on a thin manifold where x occurs in the data. Most of R n consists of adversarial examples and rubbish class examples (see the appendix). This plot was made from a naively trained maxout network. Left) A plot showing the argument to the softmax layer for each of the 10 MNIST classes as we vary ϵ on a single input example. The correct class is 4. We see that the unnormalized log probabilities for each class are conspicuously piecewise linear with ϵ and that the wrong classifications are stable across a wide region of ϵ values. Moreover, the predictions become very extreme as we increase ϵ enough to move into the regime of rubbish inputs. Right) The inputs used to generate the curve (upper left = negative ϵ , lower right = positive ϵ , yellow boxes indicate correctly classified inputs).
description:
## Description
This figure is a plot showing the effect of varying ϵ on the softmax layer's output for a single MNIST input example. The plot demonstrates that adversarial examples occur reliably for large ϵ values, while correct classifications occur only on a thin manifold. The correct class is 4, and the plot shows piecewise linear unnormalized log probabilities for each class as ϵ varies. Yellow boxes indicate correctly classified inputs.

## Text in figure
Left panel: "ϵ", "Correct class 4", "Unnormalized log probabilities", "Rubbish class examples". Right panel: "Inputs used to generate the curve", "Upper left = negative ϵ", "Lower right = positive ϵ", "Yellow boxes indicate correctly classified inputs".

caption: Figure 5: Randomly generated fooling images for a convolutional network trained on CIFAR10. These examples were generated by drawing a sample from an isotropic Gaussian, then taking a gradient sign step in the direction that increases the probability of the 'airplane' class. Yellow boxes indicate samples that successfully fool the model into believing an airplane is present with at least 50% confidence. 'Airplane' is the hardest class to construct fooling images for on CIFAR-10, so this figure represents the worst case in terms of success rate.

The yellow boxes indicate the worst-case scenario in terms of fooling success rate, as 'airplane' is the hardest class to generate fooling images for.
